content: 1. Health systems consist of people, institutions, and resources organized according to established policies to enhance the health of the population they serve. These systems aim to meet individuals' legitimate expectations while protecting them from the financial burden of illness through various health-improving activities. 2. Home care services, provided by community and home care providers, are sometimes referred to as independent social welfare associations or community and home care providers. These services typically include routine personal care, support, and assistance with daily living activities for individuals affected by aging, illness, injury, or other physical or mental conditions. Care is delivered in private homes or independent residential settings, following care plans established by health professionals. 3. Home modifications involve permanent changes to the physical features of a home to improve safety, accessibility, and comfort for its residents. 4. Hospices are facilities where end-of-life care is provided by health professionals and volunteers, either in tertiary care facilities or community health centers. They offer medical, psychological, and spiritual support to ensure that individuals nearing the end of life experience peace, comfort, and dignity. Hospice care focuses on managing pain and symptoms to keep patients as alert and comfortable as possible. These programs also provide support services for the patient’s family. 5. Hospitals are licensed establishments primarily engaged in providing medical, diagnostic, and treatment services, including physician, nursing, and other health services, to inpatients. They also offer specialized accommodation services required by inpatients. Hospitals often deliver inpatient care using advanced medical technology and professional expertise. While their primary activity is inpatient medical care, they may also provide outpatient, day care, and home health care services as secondary activities. The roles of hospitals vary by country and are defined by legal requirements. 6. The human rights of individuals with dementia include ensuring the least restrictive care, informed consent for treatment, confidentiality, avoidance of restraint and seclusion when possible, and fair procedures for admission, treatment, and discharge. These rights also encompass protection from staff abuse and safeguarding personal property. A comprehensive approach to human rights for people with dementia includes civil, political, economic, social, and cultural rights. 7. Inpatient care includes general hospitals, geriatric and psychiatric hospitals, dementia-specific and non-specific wards for long-term institutional care, palliative care units, and residential care facilities. 8. An integrated action plan addresses multiple issues within a chronic disease prevention and health promotion framework. It targets major risk factors common to chronic diseases and integrates primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention efforts across sectors and disciplines. 9. An integrated pathway is a structured and organized approach to planning, resourcing, and delivering continuous care. It defines the agreed route an individual takes through health and social care services, specifying the type of care, involved professionals, their skill levels, and the location of care delivery. 10. Legal capacity refers to an individual’s ability to act within the legal system. It is a construct created by legal systems to define the relationship between individuals and the law. Legal capacity allows individuals to access the civil and judicial system and make decisions independently. The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities recognizes the right of individuals with disabilities, including mental disabilities, to exercise their legal capacity and make decisions on all aspects of their lives on an equal basis with others. 11. Legislation refers to laws enacted by governing bodies in a country. In the context of dementia, legislation often focuses on civil and human rights protection, treatment facilities, personnel, professional training, and service structures. 12. Multisectoral approaches involve collaboration among agencies and organizations from various sectors of society, including governments, non-governmental organizations (NGOs), private for-profit entities, and civil society. 13. Noncommunicable diseases (NCDs) are not transmitted from person to person. They are typically long-lasting and progress slowly. The four main types of NCDs are cardiovascular diseases (e.g., heart attack and stroke), cancers, chronic respiratory diseases (e.g., chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and asthma), and diabetes. 14. Non-governmental organizations (NGOs) are established to benefit the public and typically operate on a not-for-profit basis. They can function at local, national, or international levels and perform various service and humanitarian functions, such as charities, missions, and consumer organizations. 15. Nurses are health professionals who have completed formal training in nursing at a recognized university-level institution, earning a diploma or degree in nursing. 16. Operational policies, strategies, or action plans are those actively implemented in a country with available resources and funding. 17. Outpatient facilities manage clinical and social care on an outpatient basis. These include hospital outpatient departments, primary health care centers, and community-based health care facilities, such as day centers. 18. Palliative care is an approach aimed at improving the quality of life for patients and their families facing life-threatening illnesses. It focuses on early identification, assessment, and treatment of pain and other physical, psychosocial, and spiritual problems. Palliative care provides relief from pain and distressing symptoms, affirms life, and regards dying as a natural process. It neither hastens nor postpones death and integrates psychological and spiritual aspects of care. It supports patients to live actively until death and helps families cope during the patient’s illness and bereavement. 19. Patient registries are systems for ongoing registration of all cases of a specific disease or health condition within a population. They provide epidemiological data, support clinical best practices, and facilitate research. At a basic level, a patient registry is a database containing information about patients' medical conditions and treatments. 20. Person-centered care focuses on organizing care around the health needs and expectations of individuals and communities rather than diseases. It extends the concept of patient-centered care to include families, communities, and society, emphasizing their role in shaping health policies and services. 21. The total number of individuals diagnosed with dementia in a given year can be calculated using various methods, such as hospital admission records, prescriptions for dementia drugs, primary care records, dedicated dementia registries, or household survey data. 22. Personal support workers provide routine care, support, and assistance with daily living activities for individuals affected by aging, illness, injury, or other physical or mental conditions. They work in private homes or independent residential settings, following care plans established by health professionals. They may also be referred to as nurse aides, personal care workers, or home health care aides. 23. Pharmaceutical personnel include pharmacists, pharmaceutical assistants, and technicians who perform tasks related to dispensing medicinal products. 24. A policy is an official statement by a government or health authority outlining the vision, values, principles, and objectives for dementia care. It establishes a broad model of action to achieve these goals. 25. A dementia action plan details the strategies and activities to implement the dementia policy. It specifies budgets, timeframes, expected outputs, targets, and indicators to assess the plan's success. 26. Primary care refers to the first level of care, generally provided in the local community. It involves generalist professionals addressing a wide range of psychological, physical, and social problems. Primary care ensures person-focused care over time, accessibility, comprehensiveness, and coordination of care. 27. A protocol is a document designed to guide decisions and criteria regarding diagnosis, management, and treatment in specific areas of healthcare. It includes evidence-based recommendations to optimize patient care. 28. Primary care doctors, also known as general practitioners or family doctors, diagnose, treat, and prevent illnesses and maintain general health. They provide comprehensive medical care to individuals, families, and communities, often coordinating care plans with other healthcare providers. 29. Psychiatrists are medical doctors with at least two years of postgraduate training in psychiatry at a recognized teaching institution. This training may include subspecialties within psychiatry. 30. Psychosocial interventions address the ongoing psychological and social needs of individuals with dementia, their caregivers, and families. These interventions may include psychoeducation, managing behavioral and psychological symptoms, promoting daily living activities, improving cognitive function, and providing caregiver support. 31. Public health services are government-funded initiatives targeting the population as a whole. They include health situation analysis, surveillance, promotion, prevention services, infectious disease control, environmental protection, disaster preparedness, and occupational health. 32. Quality of care in a health system involves improvements in six areas: effectiveness, safety, timeliness, efficiency, equity, and patient-centeredness.
